title: Hartsel Well Depth and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Hartsel wells have a 150 ft median depth, with local drilling costs shaped by fractured mountain bedrock.
h1: Hartsel, Colorado Well Depths, Yields, and Costs
intro_html:
Buying land around Hartsel means dealing with mountain bedrock, not a uniform shallow groundwater system. Records within 5 miles show a median well depth of 150 feet, but the middle half runs from 71 to 360 feet. Reported yields also vary, with a median of 7.0 gallons per minute.

Those figures are useful for planning, not a guarantee for a particular lot. Most permits identify an unnamed or fractured-bedrock aquifer, and only part of the permit record includes construction, yield, or water-level data. Check nearby wells, the Colorado DWR permit file, and site constraints before committing to a building plan.

sections.heading: Hartsel well depths reflect fractured mountain rock
sections.html:
Hartsel wells are commonly drilled into fractured granite, gneiss, or other crystalline mountain bedrock. In the local records, the median total depth is 150 feet. The middle half falls between 71 and 360 feet, while the 90th percentile is 504 feet. The deepest recorded well is 900 feet.

Depths are spread widely: 34% of reported wells are under 100 feet, another 34% are between 100 and 300 feet, and 26% fall between 300 and 600 feet. That range matters when comparing drilling bids. A bid based only on the median could be low for a lot where the first productive fracture is much deeper.

sections.heading: What Hartsel wells produce for a household
sections.html:
Among wells with a reported pump yield, the median is 7.0 gallons per minute, with the middle half between 3.0 and 10.0 gallons per minute. The records show 56% producing between 5 and 15 gallons per minute, while 29% are between 1 and 5 gallons per minute. Only 2% report less than 1 gallon per minute, and 14% report more than 15 gallons per minute.

For a typical home, a moderate well can work when the pump, pressure tank, storage, and household demand are properly matched. Do not treat a neighboring yield as a promise. Fractured rock can change sharply from one lot to the next, so ask for the well construction report and pumping information before relying on a specific flow rate.

sections.heading: Hartsel water levels and the local trend
sections.html:
Reported static water levels have a median depth of 90 feet below the surface, with the middle half between 50 and 150 feet. That is the resting water level, not the same thing as a well’s total depth or its pumping yield. A pump installer needs to account for drawdown and the finished well’s actual water level.

The decade comparison does not show a simple decline in these records. The median static level was 110 feet below the surface in the 2010s and 90 feet in the 2020s. Because only 53 wells report a static water level, use that comparison as local context rather than proof of a basin-wide rise or fall. Water-level data are especially worth checking near Como, Jefferson, and Fairplay when those areas are relevant to a property search.

sections.heading: Who has drilled around Hartsel, and when
sections.html:
Hartsel’s permit history shows continued well construction over many decades. The records include permits from the 1950s through the 2020s, with the newest permit year listed as 2025. Permit counts were 4 in the 1950s, 15 in the 1960s, 26 in the 1970s, 61 in the 1980s, 94 in the 1990s, 75 in the 2000s, 61 in the 2010s, and 85 in the 2020s.

The most active named driller in the records is Allen Drilling & Excavating Co., Inc. (Allen, Jack R.), with 99 records. Whitewater Drilling Inc (Benkufski, John D.) appears on 34, and Authorized (Pe, Pg) appears on 24. Verify current licensing, availability, and scope directly before hiring.

sections.heading: What a new Hartsel well can cost
sections.html:
Hartsel drilling is priced around fractured mountain bedrock, including granite and gneiss. The supplied local cost model uses a typical drilling rate of $65 to $100 per foot. At the local median depth of 150 feet, the drilled hole works out to about $9,800 to $15,000.

That is not the complete project price. A finished well including the pump, pressure tank, trenching, and electrical is estimated at about $15,800 to $27,000 at the median depth. Deeper drilling, difficult access, casing and grout requirements, power distance, and storage choices can move the bid beyond that range. Ask each driller to separate footage, casing, grout, testing, pump equipment, trenching, electrical, and any standby or mobilization charges.

sections.heading: Hartsel risks: contamination, low yield, and site limits
sections.html:
Low yield and a dry hole are the main uncertainties in fractured bedrock. A nearby successful well helps, but it does not prove that the same fracture crosses your lot. Only 133 wells report a pump yield, and only 303 report a total depth, so the mapped record is useful but incomplete.

Environmental screening also matters. Within about 10 miles are 4 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 73 historic mine features, and 2 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. These locations do not automatically mean a property’s water is unsafe. Test the well water through a qualified laboratory and review nearby mine, septic, and cleanup information. Confirm setbacks, access for a rig, septic suitability, and the building envelope before drilling or buying.

sections.heading: A practical Hartsel lot-buying plan
sections.html:
Start with the exact parcel, then compare wells on neighboring properties and in the same road corridor. Look for total depth, static water level, yield, use, and aquifer description rather than relying on a countywide average. In Hartsel, 71% of permits are for domestic or household use and 20% are for stock use; the permit type still needs to match your intended use and current Colorado DWR requirements.

For a new build, confirm the well permit path before finalizing the house location. Price the driveway, drilling access, well equipment, septic system, trenching, and electrical as one site plan. If water service will include more than ordinary household use, check water rights and augmentation requirements. A DWR permit review, a driller’s site assessment, and independent water testing are sensible before closing or spending on construction.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Hartsel, Colorado?
faq.a: Hartsel wells have a median reported depth of 150 feet. The middle half runs from 71 to 360 feet, while the 90th percentile is 504 feet and the deepest recorded well is 900 feet. Fractured granite and gneiss can make the productive zone unpredictable, so nearby well records are more useful than the median alone.

faq.q: What does a Hartsel well produce?
faq.a: The median reported pump yield is 7.0 gallons per minute, with the middle half between 3.0 and 10.0 gallons per minute. Records show 2% under 1 gallon per minute, 29% from 1 to 5, 56% from 5 to 15, and 14% above 15. A neighboring yield is not a guarantee for your lot.

faq.q: How much does it cost to drill a well in Hartsel?
faq.a: The local model uses $65 to $100 per foot for fractured mountain bedrock. At the 150-foot median depth, the drilled hole is about $9,800 to $15,000. A finished well with pump, tank, trenching, and electrical is estimated at $15,800 to $27,000. Deeper drilling and difficult access can increase the bid.

faq.q: Is Hartsel well water safe to drink?
faq.a: Safety cannot be determined from depth or yield. Within about 10 miles, records show 4 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 73 historic mine features, and 2 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. Test the individual well through a qualified laboratory, and review nearby mine, septic, and cleanup information before using the water for drinking.

faq.q: Are Hartsel wells getting deeper or running dry?
faq.a: The available records do not establish a general decline. Median static water level was 110 feet below the surface in the 2010s and 90 feet in the 2020s. However, only 53 wells report a static water level, so that comparison is limited. Fractured rock can produce low-yield wells or dry holes from one parcel to the next.
